city.name: Tenochtitlan
summary: In 1519 Tenochtitlan and its twin city Tlatelolco covered an island of about 13 square kilometres in the western, freshwater part of Lake Texcoco, home to perhaps 200,000 people. Spanish soldiers compared it to Venice.

Four causeways linked it to the shore, cut by wooden bridges that could be lifted. Canals ran through the city alongside the streets, busy with canoes. At its heart was a walled sacred precinct crowned by the Great Temple. Slide 'Then ⟷ Today' to see the same streets in modern Mexico City.
city.note: A reconstruction after archaeological work under modern Mexico City and the accounts of Cortés and Bernal Díaz. Shorelines, canal routes and bridge positions are approximate. House blocks are drawn schematically to show how dense the city was, not as individual surveyed buildings.

properties.name: Lake of Mexico (fresh water)
properties.description: The western part of Lake Texcoco, kept fresh by springs and rivers and by Nezahualcoyotl's dike, which held back the salty water to the east. Chinampa farming depended on it.

properties.name: Lake Texcoco (salt water)
properties.description: The larger eastern basin of the lake, brackish and prone to flooding. The brigantines fought the Mexica canoe fleet out here in 1521.

properties.name: Lakes Xochimilco and Chalco
properties.description: The southern freshwater lakes, ringed with chinampa towns. Xochimilco's 'floating gardens' are their last remnant.

properties.name: The island city
properties.description: Tenochtitlan grew from a small rocky island by reclaiming land from the lake, plot by plot, with chinampas and landfill.

images.caption: Model of the island city and its causeways

properties.name: Houses and streets
description: Ordinary families lived in single-storey adobe houses around small courtyards; nobles in two-storey stone houses, whitewashed and often with roof gardens.
Many blocks had a street on one side and a canal on the other, so goods could arrive by canoe at the back door. Each neighbourhood (calpolli) had its own temple and school.

properties.name: Ruined city
description: Cortés demolished the city block by block during the siege to fill the canals and deny cover to the defenders. By August 1521 almost nothing was standing.
The Spanish city of Mexico was laid out on the ruins in a grid of straight streets, keeping the old causeways as its main roads.

properties.name: Chinampas of Cuepopan and Moyotlan
description: Chinampas were long, narrow raised fields built up from lake mud and plant matter, anchored by willow trees and separated by canals.
Farmers grew maize, beans, squash, chillies and flowers on them, several harvests a year. They fed the city and slowly extended the island into the lake.

properties.name: Chinampas of the southern shore
properties.description: Garden plots on the southern edge of the island, crossed by small canals and walkways.

properties.name: Chinampas of Teopan
properties.description: Garden plots along the eastern shore, facing the open lake.

properties.name: Cuepopan
properties.description: The north-west quarter, 'place of the blooming of flowers'. Each of the four quarters had its own temples, markets and neighbourhood clans (calpolli).

properties.name: Atzacoalco
properties.description: The north-east quarter, between the Great Temple and Tlatelolco.

properties.name: Teopan
properties.description: The south-east quarter, 'place of the gods', also called Zoquiapan.

properties.name: Moyotlan
properties.description: The south-west quarter, 'place of mosquitoes', the largest of the four.

properties.name: Tlatelolco
properties.description: The northern twin city, founded by a breakaway group of Mexica and conquered by Tenochtitlan in 1473. Its market was the greatest in the Americas, and it was the scene of the last stand in 1521.

properties.name: Great east–west canal
properties.description: The main canal ran from the western edge of the city past the palace of Moctezuma to the open lake on the east. Canoes brought goods and tribute right into the centre. Under the Spanish it became the Acequia Real.

properties.name: Western canal
properties.description: A north–south canal through the western quarters, crossed by the Tlacopan causeway at a bridge.

properties.name: Eastern canal
properties.description: A north–south canal through the eastern quarters.

properties.name: Tezontlali canal
properties.description: The canal that marked the boundary between Tenochtitlan and Tlatelolco.

properties.name: Tlacopan causeway
description: The shortest road to the western shore, about 3 km across the water to Tlacopan. Like the other causeways it was cut by gaps with wooden bridges that could be removed in war.
On the night of 30 June 1520 the Spaniards fled along it, the Noche Triste.

images.caption: Model of the island city and its causeways

properties.name: Iztapalapa causeway
description: The great southern causeway, about 10 km long and wide enough for eight horsemen abreast, Bernal Díaz wrote. It forked at the fort of Xoloc, one arm to Iztapalapa, one to Coyoacán.
Here Moctezuma came out to meet Cortés on 8 November 1519.

images.caption: Model of the island city and its causeways

properties.name: Coyoacán causeway
properties.description: The south-western branch from Xoloc to Coyoacán. Cristóbal de Olid's division attacked along it during the siege.

images.caption: Model of the island city and its causeways

properties.name: Tepeyac causeway
properties.description: The northern road through Tlatelolco to the shrine-hill of Tepeyac, where the Basilica of Guadalupe stands today. Sandoval closed it in June 1521, sealing the city.

images.caption: Model of the island city and its causeways

properties.name: Tecpantzinco bridge
properties.description: A removable wooden bridge where the causeway crossed the western canal. In the uprising of June 1520 the Mexica lifted the bridges to trap the Spaniards.

properties.name: Tolteca Acaloco bridge
properties.description: The canal of the Toltecs. Spanish legend puts Pedro de Alvarado's famous leap across the gap near here; the street is still called Puente de Alvarado.

properties.name: Mixcoatechialtitlan bridge
properties.description: A bridge on the open-water stretch of the causeway. On the Noche Triste this gap filled with drowned men, horses and gold.

properties.name: Western shore bridge
properties.description: The last bridge before Popotla and the mainland.

properties.name: Bridge on the Iztapalapa causeway
properties.description: One of several removable bridges on the southern causeway.

properties.name: Bridge on the Iztapalapa causeway
properties.description: One of several removable bridges on the southern causeway.

properties.name: Bridge on the Tepeyac causeway
properties.description: A removable bridge on the northern causeway.

properties.name: Breach: Tecpantzinco
properties.description: With the bridge lifted, the causeway was cut. During the siege the Spaniards filled breaches by day, and the defenders reopened them by night.

properties.name: Breach: Tolteca Acaloco
properties.description: The canal of the Toltecs, open water after the bridges were removed. The Noche Triste column was trapped here.

properties.name: Breach: Mixcoatechialtitlan
properties.description: Open water where a bridge had stood.

properties.name: Breach near the western shore
properties.description: Open water where a bridge had stood.

properties.name: Breach on the Iztapalapa causeway
properties.description: Open water where a bridge had stood.

properties.name: Breach on the Iztapalapa causeway
properties.description: Open water where a bridge had stood.

properties.name: Breach on the Tepeyac causeway
properties.description: Open water where a bridge had stood.

properties.name: Chapultepec aqueduct
description: Twin channels of masonry carried fresh spring water about 5 km from Chapultepec into the city. One channel ran while the other was cleaned.
Water sellers carried it by canoe to houses across the city.

properties.name: Chapultepec aqueduct (cut)
properties.description: On 26 May 1521 Alvarado and Olid broke the aqueduct at Chapultepec. From then on the besieged city had only brackish lake water to drink.

properties.name: Dike of Nezahualcoyotl
properties.description: A 16 km barrier of stone, earth and stakes built in the 1440s under the poet-king Nezahualcoyotl of Texcoco. It protected the city from floods and kept the salt water of the eastern lake away from the chinampas.

properties.name: Great plaza
properties.description: The open square south of the sacred precinct, between the palaces. Today it is the Zócalo, the main square of Mexico City.

properties.name: Sacred precinct
description: A walled enclosure about 400 metres across, with dozens of temples, priests' schools, a ball court and a rack displaying the skulls of sacrificial victims.
Its wall, the coatepantli, was decorated with carved serpents.

properties.name: Ruins of the sacred precinct
properties.description: After the conquest the temples were pulled down and their stones reused to build the Spanish city. The Great Temple's foundations were only rediscovered in 1978, when electricity workers dug up a huge carved stone of the moon goddess Coyolxauhqui.

properties.name: Great Temple (Templo Mayor)
description: A stepped pyramid about 45 metres high, rebuilt seven times over two centuries. On top stood twin shrines: Huitzilopochtli, god of war and the sun, painted red; and Tlaloc, god of rain, painted blue.
Here war captives were sacrificed. The Toxcatl massacre of May 1520 took place in its courtyard.

properties.name: Temple of Ehecatl-Quetzalcoatl
properties.description: A round temple to the wind god, facing the Great Temple. Its circular shape was said to let the wind flow around it. Its remains lie under the cathedral's sacristy.

properties.name: Ball court
properties.description: The court for ullamaliztli, the ritual ball game, played with a heavy rubber ball that players struck with their hips.

images.caption: Model of the Great Temple, Zócalo

properties.name: Huey Tzompantli (skull rack)
properties.description: A great wooden rack of skulls of sacrificed captives, flanked by towers of skulls. Archaeologists began excavating it in 2015 under a colonial house just west of the Great Temple.

images.file: Model of the Cerimonial Center of Tenochtitlan - Templo Mayor Archeological Zone - Mexico 2024.jpg
images.caption: Model of the sacred precinct

images.caption: Model of the Great Temple, Zócalo

properties.name: Palace of Axayacatl
description: The palace of Moctezuma's father, just west of the sacred precinct. Moctezuma lodged the Spaniards here in November 1519, and they held him prisoner in it.
In a sealed room the Spaniards found the royal treasure. They fled from here on the Noche Triste.

properties.name: Palace of Moctezuma II
description: Moctezuma's 'new houses', a vast complex of halls, courtyards and gardens east of the great plaza, with council chambers, armouries and a zoo and aviary that astonished the Spaniards.
Cortés later built his own palace on the site; today it is the National Palace.

properties.name: Great Temple of Tlatelolco
properties.description: Tlatelolco's own twin-shrined pyramid. In June 1521 the defenders sacrificed captured Spaniards here in sight of their comrades. Its ruins now stand in the Plaza of the Three Cultures.

properties.name: Tlatelolco market
description: The greatest market in the Americas. Cortés wrote that more than 60,000 people came each day to buy and sell gold, feathers, cloth, cacao, maize, fish, slaves and medicinal herbs, each in its own street.
Judges sat on the spot to settle disputes and check measures.

images.file: Fragmento del Mural de Tenochtitlán en Palacio Nacional.jpg
images.caption: Diego Rivera's mural of the Tlatelolco market

properties.name: Fort of Xoloc
properties.description: A small stone fort with towers where the Iztapalapa and Coyoacán causeways met, guarding the southern approach. Cortés captured it at the start of the siege and made it his headquarters.

properties.name: Chapultepec
properties.description: 'Grasshopper hill', a wooded rock on the western shore with sacred springs that fed the aqueduct. Mexica rulers had their portraits carved into its cliffs.

properties.name: Tepetzinco
properties.description: A small rocky island with hot springs east of the city, today the Peñón de los Baños by Mexico City's airport.

properties.name: Tepepolco
properties.description: A rocky island in the salt lake. The brigantines' first battle with the Mexica canoe fleet was fought near here in May 1521.

properties.name: Tlacopan
properties.description: The third member of the Triple Alliance, on the western shore at the end of the causeway. Alvarado's division camped here during the siege.

properties.name: Coyoacán
properties.description: A lakeshore town south-west of the city, base of Olid's division in the siege, and Cortés' headquarters afterwards while Mexico City was rebuilt.

properties.name: Iztapalapa
properties.description: A rich town on the peninsula between the lakes, built partly on the water, with famous gardens. The Spaniards spent their last night here before entering Tenochtitlan.

properties.name: Tepeyac
properties.description: A hill and shrine on the northern shore at the end of the causeway, sacred to the mother goddess Tonantzin. The Basilica of Our Lady of Guadalupe stands there today.

properties.name: Azcapotzalco
properties.description: Once the capital of the Tepanec empire that ruled the valley until the Mexica and their allies overthrew it in 1428.

properties.name: Texcoco
properties.description: Second city of the Triple Alliance, famous for its poets, laws and libraries. Cortés' base for the siege; the brigantines were launched here.

properties.name: Xochimilco
properties.description: 'Place of the flower fields', a chinampa town on the southern lake.

properties.name: Chinampas of Xochimilco
properties.description: Thousands of chinampa fields fringed the southern lakes. Their produce came to the capital by canoe. Xochimilco's canals today are the last survivors of this landscape.

properties.name: Chinampas of Tlatelolco
properties.description: Garden plots on the northern edge of Tlatelolco.
